people.label: Mark Skidmore
people.sub: Morris Chair in State and Local Government Finance and Policy, Professor of Economics, Michigan State University
people.narrative: Mark Skidmore holds the Morris Chair in State and Local Government Finance and Policy at Michigan State University, where he is a Professor of Economics working in public finance, regional economics and the economics of natural disasters. In 2017, after hearing Catherine Austin Fitts assert that the Department of Housing and Urban Development had recorded $6.5 billion in undocumented adjustments, and initially assuming she had misspoken, Skidmore set his students to compiling the unsupported adjustment figures that federal Inspectors General and the Government Accountability Office had themselves published. The exercise ran from fiscal year 1998 to fiscal year 2015 and produced a summary report, co-authored with Fitts and dated September 2017, arriving at roughly $21 trillion in unsupported journal voucher adjustments at the Department of Defense and roughly $350 billion at HUD. He then co-wrote three Forbes columns with the Boston University economist Laurence Kotlikoff - December 2017, July 2018 and January 2019 - putting the number in front of a financial-markets readership. Skidmore's own methodological caution is the most valuable thing about him for this board: the report states plainly that the public Inspector General reports 'only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors', and that data could not be recovered for several years in the series. He has never claimed that $21 trillion is missing money, and the popular restatement of his work in those terms is the single most common way the black-budget argument gets destroyed in public. Used correctly - as an eighteen-year aggregate index of documentation failure at two cabinet departments, drawn entirely from the government's own audit reports - his work is the quantitative backbone of the argument that the federal ledger cannot answer the question this board asks.
people.tierRationale: Tier B: not a custody or access witness, but the author of the only systematic compilation of federal unsupported-adjustment data, drawn entirely from primary OIG and GAO documents, with the caveats stated in his own text.

people.label: Steven Aftergood
people.sub: Director, Government Secrecy Project, Federation of American Scientists (Project on Government Secrecy 1991-2021)
people.narrative: Steven Aftergood joined the Federation of American Scientists in 1989 and directed its Project on Government Secrecy from 1991 to 2021. He is the single individual most responsible for the existence of any public intelligence budget figure at all. In 1997 he was the plaintiff in a Freedom of Information Act suit against the Central Intelligence Agency - brought by FAS with the assistance of Kate Martin of the Center for National Security Studies - that forced the declassification and release of the total United States intelligence budget for the first time in fifty years: $26.6 billion for fiscal year 1997. The Director of Central Intelligence disclosed the figure again the following year, $26.7 billion for FY1998, and then stopped; disclosure did not resume until 2007, and then only because Congress compelled it by statute in section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act. In 2006 Aftergood won a further FOIA suit against the National Reconnaissance Office securing release of unclassified budget records. His awards include the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Pioneer Award, the American Library Association's James Madison Award and the Hugh M. Hefner First Amendment Award. The relevance to this board is exact: every aggregate figure in the NIP and MIP series that anyone can cite exists because one person litigated for it and then Congress codified the minimum. Everything below the aggregate remains where it was in 1949.

people.narrative: Brett A. Mansfield, Deputy Inspector General of the Department of War, appeared before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform on 13 May 2026 at a hearing titled 'DoW Financial Management: Examining Progress and New Audit Approaches'. His oral statement is the most current authoritative public account of the Department's financial condition and it contains the figure that anchors this board's money argument: unsupported adjustments of 'over $859 billion in the last two quarters of FY 25'. He reported that the Department manages more than $4.7 trillion in assets, that material weaknesses had declined from twenty-eight in FY2024 to twenty-six in FY2025, and that auditors had issued 427 fewer Notices of Findings and Recommendations than in prior years. He also announced two structural changes with direct consequences for future transparency: the number of stand-alone reporting entities will be consolidated from twenty-two to seven in fiscal year 2027, and an independent public accounting firm will assume the group auditor role, with the Office of Inspector General retaining oversight. Consolidating twenty-two audited entities into seven reduces the number of separately reported opinions, and moving the group auditor role to a contracted firm changes who holds the working papers. Neither change is presented as a transparency measure and neither is necessarily improper, but both reduce the granularity of the annual public record about the Department's money at exactly the moment that record has become the strongest documentary support for the proposition that the Department cannot account for its spending.

entities.label: SFFAS 56 - Classified Activities (FASAB, 4 October 2018)
entities.sub: Federal accounting standard authorising modification of public financial reports to protect classified information
entities.desc: Statement of Federal Financial Accounting Standards 56, 'Classified Activities', is the single most consequential documented change to the mechanics of federal financial concealment in the modern era, and it is entirely public, dated and citable. Issued by the Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board on 4 October 2018 and effective for reporting periods beginning after 30 September 2018, it does for accounting what a special access program does for information: it creates a lawful, standards-blessed route by which the numbers a citizen reads in a government financial statement need not be the numbers in the books. Paragraph 8 permits an entity to 'modify information required by other standards if the effect of the modification does not change the net results of operations or net position', to have a component reporting entity 'excluded from one reporting entity and consolidated into another reporting entity', and to apply Board Interpretations allowing further modifications. Paragraph 9 defines 'modify' with unusual candour: 'Presenting amounts associated with one financial statement line item in another financial statement line item but not presenting narrative explaining the modification', and 'Omitting required disclosures, RSI, or RSSI that would otherwise reveal classified information.' Paragraph 12 requires component entities to disclose that the standards permit such modifications while expressly forbidding them to disclose whether they applied the Statement; paragraph 13 applies the same rule government-wide, requiring only the statement that 'modifications may have been made to certain presentations' and prohibiting identification of which Interpretations were used. The Board's Basis for Conclusions explains the reasoning: identifying which entities applied the standard 'would reveal classified information' and would let users track changes over time. The Department of Defense identified the need for the standard in August 2016 - two months after the DoD Inspector General published the Army General Fund adjustments report - citing the conflict between generally accepted accounting principles and classification obligations under Executive Order 13526. The standard does not authorise misstatement of net position at the consolidated level except through the consolidation route in paragraph 8(b), and it does not restrict cleared auditors, who continue to see the unmodified figures in appropriate environments. What it authorises is precisely the thing this board is about: a published number that is deliberately in the wrong place, with no note telling the reader that it has been moved.

SFFAS 56 does not create the capability to conceal spending - appropriation-level and program-element-level concealment long predate it - but it removes the last accounting-standards obstacle to a published financial statement that is knowingly and deliberately misleading as to the location of money, and it does so with no external tripwire, because paragraph 12 forbids the entity from saying it used the standard. Reasoning: the prohibition on disclosing application is the operative feature; a permission to modify that had to be disclosed would be detectable, and this one is not.

entities.label: Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board (FASAB)

entities.desc: FASAB was created in October 1990 by the Secretary of the Treasury, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget and the Comptroller General to set generally accepted accounting principles for the federal government. It is a nine-member board sponsored by the three principals, and its pronouncements are recognised as GAAP for federal entities by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. For the purposes of this board FASAB matters for one reason: it is the body that, on 4 October 2018, issued SFFAS 56 'Classified Activities' at the instance of the Department of Defense, and thereby wrote into generally accepted accounting principles an express permission to move amounts between line items in a public financial statement without narrative explanation, and a prohibition on saying that you had done so. FASAB's own deliberative record on that standard - exposure draft, comment letters, transcripts of Board meetings - is public and is the natural next research target for anyone attempting to establish which agencies pushed for which provisions and what the Board was told about the scale of activity that would be covered.

entities.label: DoD Agency-Wide Financial Statement Audit (FY2018-present)
entities.sub: Annual full-scope audit required by the CFO Act; disclaimer of opinion every year since inception
entities.desc: The Department of Defense was made subject to the Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990 like every other major agency, and for twenty-seven years did not attempt a full-scope audit of its financial statements. The first one covered fiscal year 2018. Every full-scope audit from FY2018 through FY2025 - eight consecutive years - has ended in a disclaimer of opinion: the Inspector General has been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to express any opinion at all on whether the Department's financial statements are fairly presented. This is not a qualified opinion or an adverse opinion; it is a statement that the books cannot be audited. The FY2025 audit, reported in DOWIG-2026-081 'The FY 2025 DoW Financial Statement Audit Explained' published 12 May 2026, identified twenty-six material weaknesses across three categories - ten in management responsibility and asset accountability, six in information technology, and ten in accounting. Among the accounting weaknesses is one named 'Unsupported Accounting Adjustments', under which the report states that in the last two quarters of FY2025 the Department's adjustments totalled more than $859 billion, with contributions from the Army, Air Force, Navy and the Defense Logistics Agency across both general and working capital funds. Twenty-two reporting entities received stand-alone audits: eleven clean opinions, one qualified, nine disclaimers, and one (the Navy Working Capital Fund) no opinion under a two-year cycle. Two of the twenty-six weaknesses go directly to the question this board asks - 'Universe of Transactions', meaning the Department cannot establish the complete set of transactions falling within audit scope, and 'Fund Balance with Treasury', an account holding roughly $1 trillion that the Department cannot reconcile. An entity that cannot enumerate its own transactions cannot demonstrate the absence of any particular transaction, and that is the precise structural reason a documented audit failure is evidence in a concealment investigation rather than merely a management scandal.

entities.label: DODIG-2016-113 - Army General Fund Adjustments Not Adequately Documented or Supported
entities.sub: DoD OIG audit report, 26 July 2016; source of the $2.8 trillion and $6.5 trillion figures
entities.desc: This is the report from which the entire '$21 trillion' literature descends, and it must be quoted precisely or it becomes useless. Published 26 July 2016, it found that the Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Army (Financial Management and Comptroller) and the Defense Finance and Accounting Service Indianapolis 'did not adequately support $2.8 trillion in third quarter journal voucher (JV) adjustments and $6.5 trillion in yearend JV adjustments made to AGF data during FY 2015 financial statement compilation.' Footnote 2 of the report states that the amounts are not cumulative and should not be added together. What the figures measure is the gross dollar value of accounting entries made to force the Army General Fund's compiled data into balance, not a sum of money that went missing: the same underlying dollar can be adjusted many times in a compilation cycle, which is why the totals exceed the Army General Fund's annual appropriation by roughly two orders of magnitude. Read correctly, the report is not evidence that $6.5 trillion vanished. It is evidence of something arguably more useful to this board: that the Army's financial records for FY2015 were reconstructed at year end by trillions of dollars of entries for which no supporting documentation could be produced, and that therefore the ledger cannot be used to establish where any given appropriation actually went. Anyone citing this report for the proposition that trillions are missing will be correctly demolished; anyone citing it for the proposition that the audit trail does not exist is citing it exactly as written.

entities.desc: Mark Skidmore, an economist at Michigan State University, and Catherine Austin Fitts, a former Assistant Secretary of Housing at HUD and former managing director at Dillon Read, compiled the unsupported journal voucher adjustment figures reported in publicly available Inspector General and Government Accountability Office documents for the Department of Defense and the Department of Housing and Urban Development across fiscal years 1998 to 2015. Their summary report, dated September 2017, arrives at approximately $21 trillion for DoD and approximately $350 billion for HUD. The figure is a sum of gross adjustment amounts drawn from summary tables in OIG reports; the authors state explicitly that 'The Inspector General's reports that are available to the public only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors', and that data could not be recovered for a number of years. The number is therefore not a measure of money that went missing, was stolen, or was spent off-book, and the authors do not claim that it is. What it is, and what makes it usable, is an aggregate index of the scale at which two cabinet departments made accounting entries they could not document, sustained over eighteen years and across administrations of both parties. The figure has been repeatedly and damagingly overstated in secondary coverage as '$21 trillion missing'; that formulation is indefensible and should never be used on this board. The defensible formulation is: over eighteen fiscal years, DoD and HUD made publicly reported unsupported adjustments whose gross value totalled roughly $21 trillion, and neither department can say what those entries were for.

claims.text: Skidmore and Fitts compiled publicly reported unsupported journal voucher adjustments from OIG and GAO documents for FY1998-FY2015 and arrived at roughly $21 trillion for DoD and roughly $350 billion for HUD.

The authors state: 'The Inspector General's reports that are available to the public only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors.'
The authors state they were unable to recover data for a number of years within the FY1998-FY2015 window.

The $21 trillion figure double-counts by construction, because gross adjustment volumes across eighteen years are being summed and individual dollars are adjusted repeatedly; it is an index of documentation failure, not a quantity of money. Reasoning: it is derived from the same class of gross-entry figures as the DODIG-2016-113 $6.5 trillion number, which the OIG itself flags as non-cumulative.

entities.label: National Intelligence Program (NIP)
entities.sub: The non-DoD-controlled half of the US intelligence budget; funded across many agencies, controlled by the DNI
entities.desc: The National Intelligence Program is the intelligence budget that the Director of National Intelligence controls, as distinct from the Military Intelligence Program which the Secretary of Defense controls. Its aggregate appropriated total has been published annually since FY2007 under section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007 (Public Law 110-53), which requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate amount appropriated within thirty days of the end of each fiscal year; since February 2011 the aggregate request has also been published, under section 364 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010. Those are the only two numbers Congress has required to be made public. The appropriated toplines run from $43.5 billion in FY2007 to $73.3 billion in FY2025, with an FY2026 request of $81.9 billion. What is not published is any breakdown whatsoever: not by agency, not by programme, not by intelligence discipline, not by appropriation account. The NIP is not itself an appropriation - it is a cross-cutting programme construct whose money is appropriated inside other bills and other departments' accounts, chiefly the Department of Defense, which is the structural fact that makes the intelligence budget a concealment mechanism rather than merely a secret. A dollar appropriated in a Department of Defense account, scored to the NIP, controlled by the DNI, and executed by a contractor is a dollar with four different institutional owners and one public number.

claims.text: Section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007 (P.L. 110-53) requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate amount appropriated for the NIP within 30 days of the end of each fiscal year.
Section 364 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010 required disclosure of the aggregate NIP budget request; the first such release was in February 2011.
The FY2026 NIP budget request was $81.9 billion.
No breakdown of the NIP by agency, programme, discipline or appropriation account is published; the statutory disclosure is of the aggregate only.

entities.label: Military Intelligence Program (MIP)
entities.sub: The Secretary of Defense's intelligence budget; aggregate topline released by DoD, no breakdown
entities.desc: The Military Intelligence Program was created in 2005 by consolidating the Joint Military Intelligence Program and the Tactical Intelligence and Related Activities aggregation, placing under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence (now Intelligence and Security) the intelligence money that supports military operations, as distinct from the National Intelligence Program controlled by the DNI. The Department of Defense publishes only an aggregate topline for the MIP, in a brief annual press release, with the standing formula that no other MIP budget figures or details will be released because they remain classified. Appropriated toplines have run from $20.0 billion in FY2007 to a peak of $29.8 billion in FY2024 and $27.8 billion in FY2025, against a FY2026 request of $33.6 billion - roughly a third of the NIP in each year. The MIP matters to this board more than the NIP does, because it is the pot of money closest to the Department's own laboratories, test ranges, materiel commands and special access program enterprise, and because its governing official, USD(I&S), is also the Department's Senior Security Official with authority over the SAP system. The NIP and MIP split also creates the oversight seam that any concealed activity would exploit: NIP money is overseen by the intelligence committees, MIP money principally by the armed services committees, and a programme scored partly to each can be described truthfully to each committee in terms that leave neither with the whole.

claims.text: MIP figures were first disclosed publicly alongside NIP totals for FY2010; the Department publishes only an aggregate topline and states that other MIP budget details remain classified.

The NIP/MIP division creates a jurisdictional seam between the intelligence committees and the armed services committees that a single activity scored across both can be described to each committee without either receiving a complete account. Reasoning: the two programmes have different controlling officials (DNI and SECDEF) and different primary oversight committees, and no statute requires a reconciled cross-programme presentation to any single body.

entities.label: The Classified Annex (NDAA and Defense Appropriations)
entities.sub: Unpublished companion document carrying the force of law over classified programme funding
entities.desc: Every year Congress enacts two sets of numbers for the Department of Defense. One is printed in the United States Statutes at Large and can be read by anyone. The other is the classified annex, and it has been given, by express statutory text, exactly the same legal force. Section 8006(a) of the Department of Defense Appropriations Act for fiscal year 2026 (division of Public Law 119-75, approved 3 February 2026) provides that with regard to the programme, project and activity tables in the explanatory statement 'and the tables contained in the classified annex accompanying this Act, the obligation and expenditure of amounts appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act for those programs, projects, and activities are hereby required by law to be carried out in the manner provided by such tables to the same extent as if the tables were included in the text of this Act.' The authorisation side does the same thing: section 4001(d) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119-60, approved 18 December 2025) states simply 'Applicability to Classified Annex.--This section applies to any classified annex that accompanies this Act', section 4001(a) having just provided that a dollar amount in a funding table is thereby authorised for obligation and expenditure. The annex is prepared by the four defense committees, is not printed in the Congressional Record, is not available to members who are not on the relevant committees without arrangement, and is never published. Its contents are the programme-element-level detail for classified activity: the actual line items, the actual dollar figures, the actual programme names. Section 8059 of the FY2026 appropriations act directs the Secretary of Defense to continue providing 'a classified quarterly report ... on certain matters as directed in the classified annex accompanying this Act' - the annex is thus itself the source of reporting requirements whose subject matter is unknown to the public. This is the structure that answers the question posed at the top of this board: money reaches a programme that does not appear as a budget line because the budget line exists, is legally binding, and is in a document nobody outside a small circle has read.

claims.text: Section 8006(a), DoD Appropriations Act 2026: the tables in the classified annex accompanying the Act are 'hereby required by law to be carried out in the manner provided by such tables to the same extent as if the tables were included in the text of this Act.'

Section 4001(d), NDAA FY2026: 'Applicability to Classified Annex.--This section applies to any classified annex that accompanies this Act', where section 4001(a) authorises obligation and expenditure of any dollar amount specified in a funding table.

Section 8059, DoD Appropriations Act 2026, directs a continuing classified quarterly report to the Appropriations Defense subcommittees 'on certain matters as directed in the classified annex accompanying this Act.'

Section 5 of the NDAA FY2026 gives the joint explanatory statement printed in the Congressional Record on or about 10 December 2025 the same effect as a conference committee joint explanatory statement.

The classified annex is the single mechanism by which an activity can be simultaneously funded by law and absent from every public document, because the statutory text incorporates it by reference without reproducing it. Reasoning: section 8006(a) equates the annex tables to statutory text; no publication requirement attaches to the annex; therefore an appropriation with full legal force exists that has no public expression at any level of detail.

entities.label: The Classified Schedule of Authorizations (Intelligence Authorization Act)
entities.sub: The document in which the entire intelligence budget is actually authorised; never published
entities.desc: On the intelligence side the concealment is even cleaner, and it is stated in the statute itself. Section 6101 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (division F of Public Law 119-60) reads in its entirety: 'Funds are hereby authorized to be appropriated for fiscal year 2026 for the conduct of the intelligence and intelligence-related activities of the Federal Government.' No amount. Section 6102 then supplies the missing numbers by reference: 'The amounts authorized to be appropriated under section 6101 for the conduct of the intelligence activities of the Federal Government are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations prepared to accompany this division.' The Schedule is made available to the two Appropriations Committees and to the President; the President distributes it, or portions, within the executive branch; and section 6102(b)(3) provides that 'The President shall not publicly disclose the classified Schedule of Authorizations or any portion of such Schedule' except as provided in section 601(a) of the 9/11 Commission Act (50 U.S.C. 3306(a) - the aggregate topline), to the extent necessary to implement the budget, or as otherwise required by law. The same Act shows the technique at line level: section 6103 authorises $678,853,000 for the Intelligence Community Management Account in public text and then adds 'such additional amounts as are specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations referred to in section 6102(a).' A published number, a secret number, and a statutory instruction to the President not to reveal which is which. For a board investigating how a programme is funded without appearing anywhere, this section is the answer written by Congress in its own hand.

claims.text: Section 6101, IAA FY2026: 'Funds are hereby authorized to be appropriated for fiscal year 2026 for the conduct of the intelligence and intelligence-related activities of the Federal Government' - with no amount stated.
Section 6102(a): the amounts authorised 'are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations prepared to accompany this division.'

Section 6102(b)(3): 'The President shall not publicly disclose the classified Schedule of Authorizations or any portion of such Schedule' except under 50 U.S.C. 3306(a), to the extent necessary to implement the budget, or as otherwise required by law.
Section 6103 authorises $678,853,000 for the Intelligence Community Management Account in public text plus 'such additional amounts as are specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations.'
The classified Schedule is made available only to the two Appropriations Committees and the President, who distributes it within the executive branch.

entities.label: Section 8005 Transfer Authority (annual DoD Appropriations Act)
entities.sub: $6 billion per year of Secretary-level authority to move appropriated funds between accounts
entities.desc: Section 8005 is the standing provision of every Department of Defense Appropriations Act by which the Secretary of Defense, with the approval of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, may move money that Congress appropriated for one purpose to a different purpose. In the FY2026 Act the ceiling is $6,000,000,000; the FY2024 Act carried the same figure. The conditions are that the transfer be to 'higher priority items, based on unforeseen military requirements', that it not be used for an item Congress has denied, and that the Secretary 'notify the Congress promptly of all transfers'. Two features make it structurally important here. First, notification is after the fact - the statute requires prompt notice of transfers made, not prior approval. Second, section 8006(b) of the FY2026 Act provides that amounts specified in the explanatory-statement and classified-annex tables 'shall not be treated as subdivisions of appropriations for purposes of section 8005', with section 8005 applying only when the movement crosses appropriation accounts; the identical carve-out appears at section 4001(c) of the NDAA, which states that transfer or reprogramming of an amount in a funding table 'shall not count against a ceiling on such transfers or reprogrammings under section 1001 of this Act or any other provision of law, unless such transfer or reprogramming would move funds between appropriation accounts.' In plain terms: movement of money among the specific programmes and projects listed in the classified annex, so long as it stays inside a single appropriation account, is neither counted against the transfer ceiling nor separately reported. Section 8005 was the authority the Department used in 2019 to move $2.5 billion to border wall construction, litigation over which produced a substantial body of case law on the meaning of 'unforeseen military requirements' and 'denied by the Congress' - the only sustained judicial examination of the mechanism.

claims.text: Section 8005 of the DoD Appropriations Act 2026 permits transfer of not to exceed $6,000,000,000 of working capital funds or funds made available in the Act for military functions between appropriations or funds or any subdivision thereof, with OMB approval.

Section 8005 requires only that the Secretary 'notify the Congress promptly of all transfers made pursuant to this authority or any other authority in this Act' - notification after the fact, not prior approval.

Section 8006(b) provides that amounts in the explanatory-statement and classified-annex tables shall not be treated as subdivisions of appropriations for purposes of section 8005; section 8005 applies only when transfers occur between appropriation accounts.
The FY2024 DoD Appropriations Act (P.L. 118-47) carried the same $6,000,000,000 section 8005 ceiling and the same conditions.

The section 8006(b) carve-out means movements among classified-annex line items inside a single appropriation account are invisible both to the transfer ceiling and to the prompt-notification requirement. Reasoning: the notification duty in section 8005 attaches to transfers 'pursuant to this authority'; if the movement is not a section 8005 transfer because the annex tables are not subdivisions of appropriations, no section 8005 notice is triggered.

entities.label: Section 1001 General Transfer Authority (annual NDAA)
entities.sub: $6 billion of authorization-side transfer authority on a national-interest determination
entities.desc: The authorisation-side twin of section 8005. Section 1001 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 provides that 'Upon determination by the Secretary of Defense that such action is necessary in the national interest, the Secretary may transfer amounts of authorizations made available to the Department of Defense in this division for fiscal year 2026 between any such authorizations for that fiscal year (or any subdivisions thereof)', capped at $6,000,000,000, excluding transfers among military personnel authorisations, limited to higher-priority items, barred for items Congress denied, and subject only to a duty to 'promptly notify Congress of each transfer made'. The FY2025 NDAA (Public Law 118-159, 23 December 2024) carried the identical $6 billion ceiling and identical text. The trigger is the Secretary's own determination of the national interest; there is no external finding, no OMB concurrence on this side, and no prior notification. Read alongside section 4001(c), which exempts intra-account movements of funding-table amounts from counting against the section 1001 ceiling, the authorisation-side picture matches the appropriations-side picture: a large, self-certified, after-the-fact-reported authority to move money, sitting on top of a classified table of line items that is itself unpublished.

claims.text: Section 1001, NDAA FY2026: transfer authority on the Secretary's determination that action 'is necessary in the national interest', capped at $6,000,000,000, excluding military personnel transfers.
Section 1001(d) requires only that 'The Secretary shall promptly notify Congress of each transfer made under subsection (a).'
Section 1001 of the NDAA FY2025 (P.L. 118-159, enacted 23 December 2024) carried the identical $6,000,000,000 ceiling and identical conditions.

Section 4001(c), NDAA FY2026: transfer or reprogramming of a funding-table amount 'shall not count against a ceiling on such transfers or reprogrammings under section 1001 of this Act or any other provision of law, unless such transfer or reprogramming would move funds between appropriation accounts.'

entities.label: NDAA FY2024 Section 1687 - Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs
entities.sub: The statute that names the mechanism: special access funding and contractor IR&D
entities.desc: This is the most important single provision on this board, because it is Congress, in enacted law, naming the two mechanisms by which it believed UAP work was being funded outside its sight. Section 1687 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 (Public Law 118-31, enacted 22 December 2023) is headed 'Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs'. Subsection (a) bars obligation or expenditure of any funds authorised by the Act 'in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b), carrying the codification note '50 USC 3373 note', is headed 'Limitation Regarding Independent Research and Development' and provides that 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' The syntax of the last clause is defective in the enrolled text - 'made available the appropriate congressional committees' - which is itself worth noting as evidence of late drafting. The substance is not defective at all. Congress legislated a bar on the reimbursement, as an allowable indirect cost, of contractor-directed research relating to UAP. You do not write that sentence unless you believe such reimbursement has been happening. Subsection (a) was limited to funds authorised by that Act and therefore lapsed with fiscal year 2024; subsection (b), by its terms and by its codification as a permanent note, carries no fiscal-year limitation and remains law.

claims.text: Section 1687(a) of P.L. 118-31 bars obligation or expenditure of funds authorised by the Act on UAP activities 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' unless the Secretary of Defense has provided details to the congressional defense committees, HPSCI, SSCI and the four congressional leaders.

Section 1687(b) provides that 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership', referencing DoD Instruction 3204.01 (20 August 2014, change 2 of 9 July 2020).

Section 1687(b) carries the codification note '50 USC 3373 note' and contains no fiscal-year limitation, while section 1687(a) is limited to 'funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act'.

Congress does not enact a targeted prohibition on IR&D cost-allowability for a subject matter it believes does not exist in the IR&D portfolio. The provision is best read as a legislative acknowledgement that UAP-related work had been charged to the government as contractor independent research and development. Reasoning: IR&D allowability rules are technical and rarely legislated by subject; a subject-specific carve-out implies a specific known instance.

entities.label: IAA FY2024 Section 7343 - Funding Limitations Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena
entities.sub: The intelligence-side twin of Section 1687, running through the DNI
entities.desc: Division F of Public Law 118-31, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, contains at section 7343 the mirror image of section 1687. Subsection (b) bars obligation or expenditure of funds authorised by that division 'in support of any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation unless the Director of National Intelligence has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate committees of Congress and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' The 'appropriate committees' are defined more broadly than in section 1687: the Select and Permanent Select Committees on Intelligence, the Armed Services Committees and, notably, the Appropriations Committees of both chambers. Subsection (c) repeats the IR&D prohibition, but in the enrolled text the reference to DoD Instruction 3204.01 has been dropped, leaving the clause reading 'for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction' with no antecedent - a dangling cross-reference in enacted law. The pairing matters: Congress wrote the same funding bar twice, once for the Secretary of Defense and once for the Director of National Intelligence, which indicates the drafters did not know, or would not assume, on which side of the NIP/MIP line the activity they were legislating against sat.

claims.text: Section 7343(b) of P.L. 118-31 Division F bars use of funds authorised by that division for UAP activity under special or restricted access limitation unless the DNI has provided details to the intelligence, armed services and appropriations committees of both chambers and to congressional leadership.

Section 7343(c) repeats the IR&D indirect-cost prohibition but omits the antecedent reference to DoD Instruction 3204.01, leaving 'contracts covered by such instruction' undefined in the enrolled text.

Enacting the identical bar twice, once naming the Secretary of Defense and once naming the DNI, is consistent with congressional uncertainty as to whether the activity sits in the Military Intelligence Program or the National Intelligence Program. Reasoning: a drafter certain of the programme's home would legislate once against the controlling official.

entities.label: Independent Research and Development (IR&D) as a funding channel
entities.sub: Contractor-directed research reimbursed by the government as an allowable indirect cost
entities.desc: Independent Research and Development is the arrangement under which a defense contractor conducts research it selects, directs and owns, and charges the cost to the government as an allowable indirect expense spread across its contracts. The government pays. The contractor decides what is studied, retains the resulting intellectual property, and is not executing a contract line item that Congress appropriated by name. DoD Instruction 3204.01, dated 20 August 2014 and incorporating change 2 of 9 July 2020, sets Department policy for oversight of IR&D. There is no more precisely fitted mechanism in the federal financial system for the specific allegation this board exists to test: money reaching a private contractor's custody, funding work of the contractor's own definition, on material the contractor holds, without a congressionally identified programme line and without government ownership of the product. It is not a loophole in the sense of an oversight failure - it is a designed feature, intended to keep an industrial research base alive. What makes it evidentiary rather than merely structural is that Congress legislated against it by name in the UAP context: section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA and section 7343(c) of the FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act both provide that IR&D funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as an indirect expense unless the material and information is made available to the intelligence and defense committees and to congressional leadership. That is the named mechanism, in statute, dated 22 December 2023.

claims.text: DoD Instruction 3204.01, dated 20 August 2014 incorporating change 2 dated 9 July 2020, establishes Department policy for oversight of independent research and development.

Congress prohibited IR&D funding relating to UAP from being allowable as an indirect expense absent disclosure to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership, in both NDAA FY2024 Sec. 1687(b) and IAA FY2024 Sec. 7343(c).

IR&D is the mechanism that best fits the alleged fact pattern of government-funded, contractor-held, contractor-directed work on recovered material outside congressional programme visibility, because it combines government payment, contractor direction, contractor retention of results, and absence of a named appropriation line. Reasoning: each element of the alleged pattern maps onto a structural feature of IR&D cost allowability; no other standard federal funding instrument does so.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3510 - CIA unvouchered funds (CIA Act of 1949, sec. 8)
entities.sub: Statutory authority to spend appropriated money outside all normal accounting law
entities.desc: Enacted as section 8 of the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949 on 20 June 1949, this is the oldest and bluntest black-budget instrument in American law, and it has never been repealed or narrowed. The operative text: 'The sums made available to the Agency may be expended without regard to the provisions of law and regulations relating to the expenditure of Government funds; and for objects of a confidential, extraordinary, or emergency nature, such expenditures to be accounted for solely on the certificate of the Director and every such certificate shall be deemed a sufficient voucher for the amount therein certified.' Two clauses, two different powers. The first disapplies the whole body of federal expenditure law to Agency spending. The second provides that for confidential, extraordinary or emergency objects the Director's own signature is the entire accounting record - no receipt, no contract file, no audit trail, and by statute nothing further may be demanded. The provision dates from 1949, which places it squarely inside the period in which the alleged recovery programme is said to have been established and in which the institutional architecture of concealment was being built. Any account of how a programme could be financed for decades without appearing in any auditable record must begin here, because Congress wrote the answer in 1949 and has left it on the books ever since.

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3510(b): 'The sums made available to the Agency may be expended without regard to the provisions of law and regulations relating to the expenditure of Government funds; and for objects of a confidential, extraordinary, or emergency nature, such expenditures to be accounted for solely on the certificate of the Director and every such certificate shall be deemed a sufficient voucher for the amount therein certified.'
The provision originates as section 8 of the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949, enacted 20 June 1949.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3306 - Public disclosure of NIP aggregate amounts
entities.sub: The entire statutory transparency regime for the intelligence budget: two numbers a year, waivable
entities.desc: This section, enacted as section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act of 2007 and later supplemented for the request side by section 364 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, is the sum total of what Congress has required to be told to the public about the intelligence budget. Subsection (a): at the time the President submits the budget, he 'shall disclose to the public the aggregate amount of appropriations requested for that fiscal year for the National Intelligence Program.' Subsection (b): 'Not later than 30 days after the end of each fiscal year, the Director of National Intelligence shall disclose to the public the aggregate amount of funds appropriated by Congress for the National Intelligence Program for such fiscal year.' Subsection (c) permits the President to waive or postpone either disclosure by submitting to the intelligence committees an unclassified statement that disclosure would damage national security together with a statement of reasons that may be classified. Two aggregate numbers per year, no breakdown of any kind, and a waiver the President can exercise at will. It is worth stating plainly what this regime does not require: it does not require disclosure of the Military Intelligence Program, of any agency's budget, of any programme, of the number of programmes, or of whether any given activity is funded at all. The 9/11 Commission had recommended that the overall figure be disclosed precisely so that the public could hold the intelligence enterprise to account; what emerged in statute is the minimum reading of that recommendation.

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3306(a) requires public disclosure of the aggregate NIP appropriations request at the time the President submits the budget.
50 U.S.C. 3306(b) requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate NIP appropriated amount within 30 days of the end of each fiscal year.
50 U.S.C. 3306(c) permits the President to waive or postpone either disclosure on submitting an unclassified damage statement and a reasons statement that may be classified.

Section 6102(b)(3)(A) of the FY2026 IAA identifies 50 U.S.C. 3306(a) as the sole affirmative exception to the bar on the President publicly disclosing any portion of the classified Schedule of Authorizations.

entities.label: Line item 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' / Program Element 9999999999
entities.sub: The published, legally binding budget lines that state a number and nothing else
entities.desc: The most direct answer to how money reaches a programme that does not appear as a budget line is that it does appear as a budget line - a line whose title is the word 'CLASSIFIED' and whose only other content is a dollar figure. In the funding tables of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119-60, division D), twenty-five separate rows are titled 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS'. Summed, they carry $95.786 billion requested and $95.907 billion authorized. The largest single one is line 077A, Other Procurement, Air Force: $26,920,092 thousand - $26.92 billion of procurement money in one Air Force appropriation account, described by one word. Immediately above it sits line 077, 'SPECIAL UPDATE PROGRAM', at $1,178,397 thousand, an equally uninformative title with a long history in the Air Force budget. Other Procurement, Air Force is the account in which the intelligence community's aerial and space reconnaissance funding has historically been carried, and this row is what defense-budget analysts call the Air Force 'pass-through': money that appears in the Air Force's total obligational authority, counts against the Air Force topline, and is not spent by or controlled by the Air Force. On the research side the concealment is even more literal: classified research, development, test and evaluation appears under Program Element number 9999999999 - an all-nines placeholder in the Department's own programme element numbering system - with $22,264,031 thousand requested for the Air Force alone at line 293A in FY2026, and further nine-nines rows in the Navy ($2,554,769 thousand at line 259A) and Special Operations ($8,276,313 thousand at line 298A). Operation and Maintenance, Defense-Wide carries $22,750,830 thousand at line 530A; Operation and Maintenance, Army carries $2,385,523 thousand at line 590A. The three-year series computed directly from the enacted funding tables runs: FY2024, twenty-two rows, $86.912 billion authorized; FY2025, twenty-four rows, $88.682 billion; FY2026, twenty-five rows, $95.907 billion. These are the visible edges of the black budget. What they fund is in the classified annex.

entities.label: Section 8009 - 30-day advance notice before initiating or materially modifying a special access program
entities.sub: Appropriations-side SAP tripwire; the companion to 10 U.S.C. 119
entities.desc: Section 8009 of the Department of Defense Appropriations Act for fiscal year 2026 provides, in a single sentence: 'Funds appropriated by this Act may not be used to initiate, or materially modify the scope of, a special access program without prior notification 30 calendar days in advance to the congressional defense committees.' It is the appropriations-side companion to the authorisation-side reporting regime of 10 U.S.C. 119, and it is a purer instrument, because it attaches to the money rather than to a reporting duty and because it contains no waiver. A programme initiated with funds appropriated by that Act without the 30-day notice is a programme operating on funds the statute says may not be used for it. This is the provision against which any concealed UAP-related special access programme would have to be measured, and it is also the provision that a programme predating 1988 - or funded from sources other than annual DoD appropriations, such as contractor IR&D reimbursement or the CIA's unvouchered account under 50 U.S.C. 3510 - would not touch at all.

claims.text: Section 8009, DoD Appropriations Act 2026: 'Funds appropriated by this Act may not be used to initiate, or materially modify the scope of, a special access program without prior notification 30 calendar days in advance to the congressional defense committees.'

Section 8009 binds only funds appropriated by that Act, so it does not reach an activity financed through contractor independent research and development reimbursement, through unvouchered CIA funds under 50 U.S.C. 3510, or through prior-year balances. Reasoning: the prohibition is drafted as a limitation on the use of that Act's appropriations, not as a general prohibition on unnotified SAPs.

entities.label: Section 8084 - NIP reprogramming notification against classified annex levels

entities.desc: Section 8084(b) of the FY2026 Department of Defense Appropriations Act provides that no funds for the National Intelligence Program in that or any prior appropriations Act 'shall be available for obligation or expenditure through a reprogramming or transfer of funds in accordance with section 102A(d) of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 3024(d)) that results in a cumulative increase or decrease of the levels specified in the classified annex accompanying the Act unless the congressional intelligence committees are notified 30 days in advance of such reprogramming of funds', and adds that 'this notification period may be reduced for urgent national security requirements.' It is worth reading what this establishes rather than what it restricts. It establishes, in public statutory text, that the operative funding levels for the National Intelligence Program are 'the levels specified in the classified annex' - not the levels in the printed bill, which do not exist for the NIP at all. It establishes that the DNI's transfer and reprogramming authority under 50 U.S.C. 3024(d) operates against that unpublished baseline. And it establishes that the notification period, already only thirty days and only to two committees, may be shortened at the executive's assessment of urgency.

claims.text: Section 8084(b), DoD Appropriations Act 2026, conditions NIP reprogramming or transfer under 50 U.S.C. 3024(d) that cumulatively increases or decreases 'the levels specified in the classified annex accompanying the Act' on 30 days advance notice to the congressional intelligence committees.
The same subsection provides that 'this notification period may be reduced for urgent national security requirements.'

entities.label: The misappropriation allegation: Grusch's ICIG complaint and sworn testimony
entities.sub: May 2022 ICIG urgent-concern complaint; 26 July 2023 sworn testimony to House Oversight
entities.desc: The specific allegation that programme funds were moved into private contractor custody outside congressional oversight has a named source, a date, a legal vehicle and an oath. David Charles Grusch, formerly the National Reconnaissance Office's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force and a senior technical adviser on UAP analysis at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, filed a Disclosure of Urgent Concern and Complaint of Reprisal with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in May 2022, through counsel Charles McCullough III - himself a former Intelligence Community Inspector General. The ICIG found the complaint credible and urgent in July 2022. Grusch then briefed the staffs of the congressional intelligence committees in closed session. On 5 June 2023 he went on the record with Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal in The Debrief, stating: 'Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia.' That sentence is the named mechanism: not a generic accusation of secrecy but a specific claim of procurement fraud - contracting conducted outside the Federal Acquisition Regulation, which is the body of law governing how the government buys things and what the government owns when it has paid. On 26 July 2023 Grusch testified under oath before the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs of the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, at a hearing titled 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency', alongside Ryan Graves and Commander David Fravor. His written statement records that he was 'informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program' to which he was denied access, and refers to 'Non-Human Reverse Engineering Programs'; the specific financial detail he declined to give in open session, offering it in a classified setting. Five months later Congress enacted section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA, barring funds for unreported UAP special access activity and barring UAP-related contractor independent research and development from being an allowable indirect cost. The sequence - complaint, credible-and-urgent finding, closed briefings, sworn testimony, statute naming IR&D - is the strongest documented chain on this board connecting an allegation about money to legislative action about money.

claims.text: Grusch, quoted in The Debrief on 5 June 2023: 'Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia.'
Charles McCullough III filed a Disclosure of Urgent Concern(s) and Complaint of Reprisal on Grusch's behalf with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in May 2022.
The Intelligence Community Inspector General found the complaint 'credible and urgent' in July 2022.

Grusch testified under oath on 26 July 2023 before the House Oversight subcommittee at the hearing 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency', with Ryan Graves and David Fravor.

Grusch's written testimony states he was 'informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program' to which he was denied access, and refers to 'Non-Human Reverse Engineering Programs'.

Grusch's written testimony to the House Oversight Committee contains no discussion of funding mechanisms, budget lines, or contractor financial arrangements; the financial specifics were reserved for classified session.

The named mechanism in the allegation is procurement rather than appropriation: 'illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations' describes government money reaching a contractor under an instrument that does not comply with the rules determining what the government gets for it - which is the precise legal condition under which recovered material could sit in private custody while having been paid for with federal funds. Reasoning: the FAR governs data rights, property title and cost allowability; contracting outside it is how title would fail to pass.

entities.label: NDAA FY2026 UAP provisions (Secs. 1671-1673)

entities.desc: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 was approved on 18 December 2025. Its UAP provisions run in two opposite directions at once and both matter to the money question. Section 1672, 'Elimination of Duplicative Reporting Requirements Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena', repeals section 413 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373a) outright, and rewrites section 1683(f)(1)(A) of the FY2022 NDAA so that the DNI and the Secretary of Defense 'shall jointly require that each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena makes such data available immediately to the Office in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods.' Section 1673, 'Accounting of Security Classification Guides Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena', directs the Director of AARO within 180 days of enactment - by roughly 16 June 2026 - to make an accounting of the security classification guides that apply to information used for UAP reports and investigations, and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix. Section 1671 requires briefings on intercepts of UAP by NORAD and USNORTHCOM. What is absent is as important as what is present: neither the FY2025 nor the FY2026 NDAA re-enacted the section 1687(a) bar on funds for unreported UAP special access activity, which by its terms applied only to funds authorised by the FY2024 Act. The permanent piece - the IR&D indirect-cost prohibition at section 1687(b), codified as a 50 U.S.C. 3373 note - survives; the annual funding bar did not.

entities.label: Reprogramming of DoD Appropriated Funds (DoD FMR Volume 3, Chapter 6; DD Form 1415 series)
entities.sub: The administrative machinery for moving money after appropriation, including below-threshold reprogramming
entities.desc: Below the statutory transfer authorities sits an administrative layer that does most of the actual work. Volume 3, Chapter 6 of the Department of Defense Financial Management Regulation, 'Reprogramming of DoD Appropriated Funds', dated September 2015, establishes four categories of action. Prior Approval Reprogramming, on DD Form 1415-1, requires written approval from the congressional committees before execution and covers major decisions and items of special congressional interest. Letter Notification, DD Form 1415-2, gives Congress thirty days advance notice with an opportunity to object. Internal Reprogramming, DD Form 1415-3, is an audit-trail action processed entirely within the Department for reclassifications between line items where the substance of the programme is unchanged. And Below-Threshold Reprogramming requires no approval and no notification at all: components may realign funds within prescribed cumulative annual limits at their own discretion. The thresholds at which congressional approval becomes necessary are: $10 million for Military Personnel, $15 million for Operation and Maintenance, $20 million or 20 percent of the programme base (whichever is less) for Procurement, and $10 million or 20 percent of the programme base (whichever is less) for Research, Development, Test and Evaluation. Against a Department managing more than $4.7 trillion in assets and executing hundreds of billions of dollars annually, a $10 million RDT&E threshold means that an enormous volume of money moves each year with no external record generated at all. This is the layer at which the audit trail is thinnest and at which the $859 billion of unsupported adjustments reported for the last two quarters of FY2025 lives.

claims.text: DoD FMR Volume 3 Chapter 6, 'Reprogramming of DoD Appropriated Funds' (September 2015), establishes Prior Approval Reprogramming (DD 1415-1), Letter Notification (DD 1415-2), Internal Reprogramming (DD 1415-3) and Below-Threshold Reprogramming.
Below-Threshold Reprogramming permits components to realign funds within prescribed cumulative annual limits without approval or notification.

Congressional approval thresholds: Military Personnel $10 million; Operation and Maintenance $15 million; Procurement $20 million or 20 percent of programme base, whichever is less; RDT&E $10 million or 20 percent of programme base, whichever is less.
Internal Reprogramming on DD Form 1415-3 is processed entirely within the Department as an audit-trail action, with no congressional action required.

It sits alongside four other Department of Defense entries: Weapon Systems Acquisition, which regressed; Approach to Business Transformation; Business Systems Modernization; and Contract Management. Five of the roughly three dozen government-wide high-risk areas are Department of Defense entries, and the money-related ones have been there without resolution across six presidential administrations. The significance for this board is not that the Department wastes money - every large organisation does - but that the Comptroller General of the United States has certified, repeatedly and in writing, that the Department's financial management systems cannot produce reliable information. entities.label: The intelligence budget disclosure record, FY1997-FY2026
entities.sub: Every published NIP and MIP figure, and the litigation and statutes that produced them
entities.desc: The complete public record of what the United States spends on intelligence consists of two numbers per year, and it exists in two segments separated by a nine-year gap. The first segment was created by litigation: following a FOIA suit brought by the Federation of American Scientists with the assistance of Kate Martin of the Center for National Security Studies, the Director of Central Intelligence declassified the total intelligence budget for the first time in fifty years in 1997 - $26.6 billion for FY1997 - and again in 1998 - $26.7 billion for FY1998. Then disclosure stopped. Nothing further was released until 2007, when the newly created Director of National Intelligence began publishing the National Intelligence Program aggregate under statutory compulsion. Military Intelligence Program figures were first published alongside the NIP for FY2010. The combined series, as compiled by the FAS Intelligence Resource Program: FY2007 $43.5bn NIP and $20bn MIP, total $63.5bn; FY2008 $47.5/$22.9/$70.4; FY2009 $49.8/$26.4/$76.2; FY2010 $53.1/$27.0/$80.1; FY2011 $54.6/$24.0/$78.6; FY2012 $53.9/$21.5/$75.4; FY2013 $52.7/$19.2/$71.9; FY2014 $50.5/$17.4/$67.9; FY2015 $50.3/$16.5/$66.8; FY2016 $53.0/$17.7/$70.7; FY2017 $54.6/$18.4/$73.0; FY2018 $59.4/$22.1/$81.5; FY2019 $60.2/$21.5/$81.7; FY2020 $62.7/$23.1/$85.8; FY2021 $60.8/$23.3/$84.1; FY2022 $65.7/$24.1/$89.8; FY2023 $71.7/$27.9/$99.6; FY2024 $76.5/$29.8/$106.3; FY2025 $73.3/$27.8/$101.1; and for FY2026 a request of $81.9bn NIP and $33.6bn MIP. That is the whole of it. There is no agency line, no programme line, no discipline line and no reconciliation to the Department of Defense budget in which most of the money is appropriated.

claims.text: The 1997 disclosure of $26.6 billion for FY1997 was the first release of the total US intelligence budget in fifty years and followed FOIA litigation brought by FAS with the assistance of Kate Martin of the Center for National Security Studies.
The DCI disclosed $26.7 billion for FY1998 and then ceased disclosure; publication did not resume until the DNI released the FY2007 NIP figure.
MIP figures were first disclosed alongside NIP totals for FY2010.
The FY2026 request was $81.9 billion NIP and $33.6 billion MIP.

The published intelligence aggregate cannot be reconciled to the published defense budget by any external party, because NIP and MIP money is appropriated inside Department of Defense accounts whose classified line items are not broken out.
