timeline.label: CIA Act of 1949 creates unvouchered spending
timeline.text: Section 8 of the Central Intelligence Agency Act, now 50 U.S.C. 3510(b), permits Agency sums to be 'expended without regard to the provisions of law and regulations relating to the expenditure of Government funds', with confidential, extraordinary or emergency objects 'accounted for solely on the certificate of the Director'. The oldest and bluntest black-budget instrument in American law, enacted two years after Roswell and never narrowed.

timeline.label: Chief Financial Officers Act; FASAB created
timeline.text: The CFO Act imposes audited financial statements on major federal agencies. In the same month the Secretary of the Treasury, the Director of OMB and the Comptroller General create the Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board to set federal accounting standards. The Department of Defense will not attempt a full-scope audit for twenty-seven years.

timeline.label: First intelligence budget disclosure in fifty years
timeline.text: Following FOIA litigation brought by the Federation of American Scientists with Steven Aftergood as plaintiff, assisted by Kate Martin of the Center for National Security Studies, the Director of Central Intelligence declassifies the total intelligence budget: $26.6 billion for FY1997. It is the first such disclosure since the CIA was created.

timeline.label: Second and last DCI disclosure, then nine years of silence
timeline.text: The DCI discloses $26.7 billion for FY1998 and then stops. No intelligence budget figure is published again until 2007, and then only because Congress compels it by statute.

timeline.label: Military Intelligence Program created
timeline.text: The Joint Military Intelligence Program and Tactical Intelligence and Related Activities aggregations are consolidated into the Military Intelligence Program under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, formalising the split between DNI-controlled and SECDEF-controlled intelligence money and creating the oversight seam between the intelligence and armed services committees.

timeline.label: FAS wins FOIA suit against the NRO
timeline.text: Aftergood, for FAS, secures release of unclassified National Reconnaissance Office budget records - the only occasion on which any component-level intelligence budget material has been prised loose by litigation.

timeline.label: Section 601 compels annual NIP disclosure
timeline.text: Section 601 of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3306, requires the DNI to disclose the aggregate NIP appropriation within 30 days of each fiscal year's end, subject to a presidential waiver. The FY2007 figure is $43.5 billion. This remains, with the later request-side requirement, the entire statutory transparency regime for the intelligence budget.

timeline.label: MIP topline published for the first time
timeline.text: Military Intelligence Program figures are disclosed alongside the NIP for FY2010: $27.0 billion MIP against $53.1 billion NIP, a combined $80.1 billion. No breakdown of either accompanies the figures, then or since.

timeline.label: First publication of the NIP budget request
timeline.text: Under section 364 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, the aggregate NIP budget request is published for the first time, in February 2011. Two numbers a year is now the settled floor and ceiling of public knowledge.

timeline.label: The only public view inside the black budget
timeline.text: The Washington Post publishes excerpts from the 'National Intelligence Program Summary for FY2013', classified TS/SI/TK/NOFORN, from the Snowden material. For the same year the officially disclosed figure was a single aggregate: $52.7 billion requested, $49.0 billion after sequestration. Thirteen years later this remains the only occasion on which the interior of the intelligence budget has been seen outside the cleared community.

timeline.label: DoD FMR Volume 3 Chapter 6 reissued
timeline.text: The Department's reprogramming regulation sets the four action types and the congressional approval thresholds - $10 million for military personnel, $15 million for operation and maintenance, $20 million or 20 percent for procurement, $10 million or 20 percent for RDT&E - and preserves Below-Threshold Reprogramming, which requires no approval and no notification at all.

timeline.label: DODIG-2016-113: $6.5 trillion in unsupported year-end adjustments
timeline.text: The DoD Inspector General finds that the Army Comptroller's office and DFAS Indianapolis 'did not adequately support $2.8 trillion in third quarter journal voucher (JV) adjustments and $6.5 trillion in yearend JV adjustments made to AGF data during FY 2015 financial statement compilation'. Footnote 2 states the amounts are not cumulative. The report will become the load-bearing citation of the entire missing-money literature, usually misquoted.

timeline.label: DoD asks FASAB for a classified-reporting standard
timeline.text: Two months after the Army adjustments report, the Department of Defense identifies to the Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board the need for a standard reconciling generally accepted accounting principles with classification obligations under Executive Order 13526. That request becomes SFFAS 56.

timeline.label: Skidmore and Fitts publish the unsupported-adjustment compilation
timeline.text: Mark Skidmore of Michigan State University and Catherine Austin Fitts publish a summary report compiling unsupported journal voucher adjustments reported in public OIG and GAO documents for FY1998-FY2015: roughly $21 trillion at DoD and $350 billion at HUD. The authors state that the public reports 'only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors'.

timeline.label: First Kotlikoff-Skidmore Forbes column
timeline.text: 'Has Our Government Spent $21 Trillion of Our Money without Telling Us?' puts the aggregate in front of a financial-markets readership. Two further columns follow in July 2018 and January 2019, the second asking directly whether the concealment is intentional.

timeline.label: FASAB issues the exposure draft for SFFAS 56
timeline.text: The exposure draft of what becomes SFFAS 56 is issued on 14 December 2017 with comments requested by 16 March 2018. FASAB receives seventeen responses from preparers, auditors and professional associations. Seventeen comment letters is the entirety of the public deliberation on a standard authorising modified public financial reporting across the federal government.

timeline.label: SFFAS 56 effective date
timeline.text: The standard takes effect for reporting periods beginning after 30 September 2018 - the first period following the Department of Defense's first full-scope financial statement audit.

timeline.label: SFFAS 56 'Classified Activities' issued
timeline.text: FASAB issues the standard permitting an entity to present amounts associated with one financial statement line item in another 'but not presenting narrative explaining the modification', to omit disclosures that would reveal classified information, and to move a component reporting entity from one consolidation to another. Paragraph 12 requires entities to disclose that such modifications are permitted while expressly forbidding them to disclose that they applied the Statement.

timeline.label: First full-scope DoD audit: disclaimer of opinion
timeline.text: David L. Norquist, Under Secretary of Defense (Comptroller) and Chief Financial Officer, writes in the FY2018 Agency Financial Report: 'In FY 2018, the Department underwent its first full-scope financial statement audit. As anticipated, our independent auditor, the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General, issued a Disclaimer of Opinion as the result of the audit.' It will be the first of eight.

timeline.label: Grusch files the ICIG urgent-concern complaint
timeline.text: Charles McCullough III, himself a former Intelligence Community Inspector General, files a Disclosure of Urgent Concern(s) and Complaint of Reprisal with the ICIG on behalf of David Grusch, covering information Grusch had gathered from 2019.

timeline.label: ICIG finds the complaint credible and urgent
timeline.text: The Intelligence Community Inspector General determines the complaint credible and urgent - the statutory finding that obliges transmission to the congressional intelligence committees.

timeline.label: Grusch names the mechanism on the record
timeline.text: In The Debrief, Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal quote Grusch: 'Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia.' Procurement fraud, not merely secrecy, is the accusation.

timeline.label: Grusch testifies under oath to House Oversight
timeline.text: At 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency', Grusch testifies alongside Ryan Graves and David Fravor. His written statement describes a 'multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program' to which he was denied access and refers to 'Non-Human Reverse Engineering Programs'. It contains no funding detail; that he reserved for classified session.

timeline.label: Congress bars UAP-related IR&D as an allowable indirect cost
timeline.text: Section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA bars funds for UAP activity under special or restricted access limitation absent disclosure to the defense and intelligence committees and congressional leadership, and provides that 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses'. Section 7343 of the Intelligence Authorization Act enacts the same bar through the Director of National Intelligence. Congress has named the mechanism.

timeline.label: AARO Historical Record Report Volume I is silent on money
timeline.text: The Pentagon's report on the historical record addresses retrieval and reverse-engineering claims at length and contains no discussion of misappropriated funds, illegal contracting, independent research and development, or contractor financial arrangements. The official rebuttal does not engage the financial allegation at all.

timeline.label: FY2025 NDAA sunsets the Historical Record Report audit requirement
timeline.text: Section 6802 of the FY2025 NDAA ties the quarterly and semiannual audit and reporting requirements on the UAP Historical Record Report to 90 and 180 days after delivery of the final volume. The same Act does not re-enact the section 1687(a) funding bar, which lapsed with fiscal year 2024.

timeline.label: FY2026 NDAA: classified annex given statutory force; UAP reporting trimmed
timeline.text: Public Law 119-60 is approved. Section 4001(d) applies the funding-table authorisation to 'any classified annex that accompanies this Act'; section 6102 provides that intelligence amounts 'are those specified in the classified Schedule of Authorizations' which the President 'shall not publicly disclose'. Section 1672 repeals 50 U.S.C. 3373a; section 1673 orders AARO to inventory the security classification guides covering UAP within 180 days.

timeline.label: FY2026 Defense Appropriations Act enacted
timeline.text: Public Law 119-75 is approved. Section 8005 carries $6 billion of transfer authority; section 8006(a) gives the classified annex tables the force of statutory text; section 8006(b) exempts annex line items from the transfer ceiling; section 8009 requires 30 days notice before initiating or materially modifying a special access program; section 8084(b) makes 'the levels specified in the classified annex' the baseline for NIP reprogramming.

timeline.label: Terry K. Patton becomes FASAB chairman
timeline.text: Patton, professor emeritus at Midwestern State University, takes the chair of the body that owns SFFAS 56 and alone can withdraw it or issue the Interpretations under paragraph 8(c) authorising further unspecified modifications to public financial reports.

timeline.label: Eighth consecutive disclaimer; $859 billion unsupported in two quarters
timeline.text: DOWIG-2026-081, 'The FY 2025 DoW Financial Statement Audit Explained', records a disclaimer of opinion for the eighth consecutive year, twenty-six material weaknesses including 'Unsupported Accounting Adjustments', 'Universe of Transactions' and 'Fund Balance with Treasury', and states that in the last two quarters of FY2025 the Department's adjustments exceeded $859 billion.

timeline.label: Deputy IG testifies to House Oversight on the $859 billion
timeline.text: Brett A. Mansfield tells the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform that unsupported adjustments exceeded $859 billion in two quarters, that the Department manages more than $4.7 trillion in assets, and that reporting entities will consolidate from twenty-two to seven in FY2027 with an independent public accounting firm taking the group auditor role. It is the same committee that heard David Grusch in July 2023.

how-money-reaches-an-invisible-program.desc: The mechanism, end to end, in six steps, each of which is documented in enacted law. (1) AUTHORISATION. Section 4001(a) of the FY2026 NDAA authorises obligation and expenditure of any dollar amount specified in a funding table; section 4001(d) provides that the section 'applies to any classified annex that accompanies this Act'. On the intelligence side, section 6101 of the FY2026 Intelligence Authorization Act authorises appropriations for intelligence activities without stating any amount, and section 6102(a) supplies the amounts by reference to 'the classified Schedule of Authorizations prepared to accompany this division', which section 6102(b)(3) forbids the President to disclose. (2) APPROPRIATION. Section 8006(a) of the FY2026 Defense Appropriations Act provides that the tables in the classified annex are 'hereby required by law to be carried out in the manner provided by such tables to the same extent as if the tables were included in the text of this Act'. (3) PUBLIC EXPRESSION. What appears in the printed law is a row saying 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' and a number - twenty-five of them in FY2026, totalling $95.9 billion authorised, the largest being $26.92 billion in Other Procurement, Air Force - or, for research, the all-nines Program Element 9999999999. (4) MOVEMENT. Section 8005 permits $6 billion of transfer with OMB approval and after-the-fact notice; section 1001 permits $6 billion on the Secretary's own national-interest determination; section 8006(b) and section 4001(c) exempt movements among annex line items inside a single appropriation account from counting against either ceiling; and beneath all of it, DoD FMR Volume 3 Chapter 6 permits Below-Threshold Reprogramming with no approval and no notification, with congressional approval thresholds as low as $10 million. (5) EXECUTION TO A CONTRACTOR. Independent Research and Development, governed by DoD Instruction 3204.01, reimburses contractor-selected, contractor-directed, contractor-owned research as an allowable indirect cost across a contract portfolio - government money, no named programme line, no government title to the result. (6) REPORTING. SFFAS 56 permits the resulting figures to be presented in a different financial statement line item with no narrative explanation, permits omission of disclosures that would reveal classified information, and forbids the entity to disclose that it applied the standard. Every step is public law or public policy. Nothing here is speculative. The only thing missing is the content of the annex.

the-21-trillion-stated-precisely.desc: This must be said once, exactly, and then never loosely. The primary document is DODIG-2016-113, published 26 July 2016, which found that the Army Comptroller's office and DFAS Indianapolis 'did not adequately support $2.8 trillion in third quarter journal voucher (JV) adjustments and $6.5 trillion in yearend JV adjustments made to AGF data during FY 2015 financial statement compilation'. Footnote 2 of the report states that the amounts are not cumulative and should not be added together. A journal voucher adjustment is an accounting entry made during compilation to force data into balance; the same underlying dollar can be adjusted many times in a cycle, which is why $6.5 trillion is roughly fifty times the Army General Fund's annual appropriation. The figure is therefore a measure of entry volume, not of money that went missing. Mark Skidmore and Catherine Austin Fitts, in a summary report dated September 2017, compiled figures of this class from published OIG and GAO documents for fiscal years 1998 through 2015 and arrived at roughly $21 trillion for the Department of Defense and roughly $350 billion for HUD. Their own text states that the public reports 'only provide summary information; thus it is impossible for us to conduct a detailed assessment of the nature of these unsupported adjustments and errors' and that data could not be recovered for several years in the series. Neither the OIG nor Skidmore and Fitts claim that $21 trillion is missing. WHAT YOU MAY SAY: over eighteen fiscal years, two cabinet departments made accounting entries with a gross value of roughly $21 trillion that they could not document, and the government's own auditors said so. WHAT YOU MAY NOT SAY: $21 trillion is missing, unaccounted for in the sense of gone, or was spent on secret programmes. The second formulation is false, is trivially rebutted, and every time it is used it discredits the first, which is true and is devastating. The current equivalent figure, from the FY2025 audit, is more than $859 billion in unsupported adjustments in two quarters - a number that requires no interpretation at all.

sffas-56-what-it-actually-permits.desc: Read the operative words. Paragraph 9(a) of SFFAS 56 defines a permitted modification as 'Presenting amounts associated with one financial statement line item in another financial statement line item but not presenting narrative explaining the modification.' Paragraph 9(b) permits 'Omitting required disclosures, RSI, or RSSI that would otherwise reveal classified information.' Paragraph 8(b) permits a component reporting entity to be 'excluded from one reporting entity and consolidated into another reporting entity' - and the Statement acknowledges that consolidation modifications 'may change the net results of operations and/or net position' of the affected entities. Paragraph 8(c) permits application of Board Interpretations allowing further, unspecified modifications. Paragraph 12 requires a component entity to disclose that the standards permit modifications and simultaneously provides that the entity 'must not disclose application of this Statement'. Paragraph 13 requires the government-wide report to say only that 'modifications may have been made to certain presentations', without identifying which Interpretations were applied. FASAB's basis for conclusions explains that identifying which entities applied the standard 'would reveal classified information' and would allow users to track changes over time. Three things follow. First, the standard is not a licence to fabricate a bottom line: except through the consolidation route, modifications must not change net results of operations or net position. Second, it is a licence to put a true number in a false place with no footnote. Third, and decisively, there is no tripwire: because paragraph 12 forbids disclosure of application, no reader of any federal financial statement can determine whether what they are reading has been modified. The standard was issued 4 October 2018, effective for periods beginning after 30 September 2018, at the request of the Department of Defense which raised the need in August 2016. The exposure draft was issued 14 December 2017 with comments due 16 March 2018; seventeen comment letters were received.

the-named-mechanism.desc: The allegation is that programme funds were moved into private contractor custody outside congressional oversight. Its named mechanism, on the record from the witness, is procurement rather than appropriation. David Grusch, quoted in The Debrief on 5 June 2023: 'Individuals on these UAP programs approached me in my official capacity and disclosed their concerns regarding a multitude of wrongdoings, such as illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations and other criminality and the suppression of information across a qualified industrial base and academia.' The Federal Acquisition Regulation is the body of rules determining what the government gets when it pays: data rights, technical data, title to property, allowability of costs. Contracting outside it is precisely how the government could pay for something and not own it. Congress then named a specific instrument. Section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA, enacted 22 December 2023 and codified as a 50 U.S.C. 3373 note, provides that 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction' - the instruction being DoD Instruction 3204.01 - 'unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership'. Section 7343(c) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024 repeats it through the Director of National Intelligence. IR&D is contractor-selected, contractor-directed research, owned by the contractor, reimbursed by the government as an overhead cost spread across a contract portfolio, with no appropriated programme line of its own. It is the only standard federal funding instrument that produces, by design, exactly the fact pattern alleged. Congress does not write a subject-specific carve-out to a cost-allowability rule about a subject it believes is absent from the IR&D portfolio. The companion funding bar in section 1687(a) - no funds for UAP activity under special or restricted access limitation absent disclosure to the committees and leadership - applied only to funds authorised by the FY2024 Act and was not re-enacted in the FY2025 or FY2026 NDAAs. The IR&D provision, having no fiscal-year limit, remains law and has never been the subject of a published compliance finding by any Inspector General.

why-the-failed-audit-is-evidence.desc: A failed audit is normally a management story. Here it is an evidentiary one, and the reason is a single named material weakness. Among the twenty-six weaknesses in the FY2025 audit is 'Universe of Transactions', which the Inspector General defines as 'The complete set of all transactions that fall within the scope of what is audited'. The Department's inability to establish that set is itself the finding. The consequence is precise and inescapable: no one - not the Inspector General, not the Government Accountability Office, not a congressional committee, not the Department itself - can demonstrate that a given payment did not occur, because the population against which such a search would run does not exist in complete form. The same audit finds Fund Balance with Treasury, roughly $1 trillion in spending accounts, unreconcilable, and 'Unsupported Accounting Adjustments' running to more than $859 billion in two quarters. The Department has now received a disclaimer of opinion for eight consecutive years, FY2018 through FY2025. In FY2025 twenty-two entities received stand-alone audits: eleven clean, one qualified, nine disclaimers, one no opinion. From FY2027 those twenty-two become seven, and an independent public accounting firm takes over as group auditor. This does not prove that anything was concealed. It proves that the instrument that would be required to disprove concealment does not exist and, on the Department's own account, has never existed.

the-classified-programs-arithmetic.desc: Computed directly from the enacted funding tables in Division D of each National Defense Authorization Act, counting every row whose title is 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS'. FY2024 (P.L. 118-31): 22 rows, $86.574 billion requested, $86.912 billion authorized. FY2025 (P.L. 118-159): 24 rows, $89.566 billion requested, $88.682 billion authorized. FY2026 (P.L. 119-60): 25 rows, $95.786 billion requested, $95.907 billion authorized. The largest single row in each year is the Air Force's Other Procurement classified line - FY2024 line 072A at $25.456 billion, FY2025 line 064A at $25.476 billion requested and $25.048 billion authorized, FY2026 line 077A at $26.920 billion. The next largest are Operation and Maintenance Defense-Wide (FY2026 line 530A, $22.751 billion) and Air Force RDT&E under Program Element 9999999999 (FY2026 line 293A, $22.264 billion requested, $22.385 billion authorized). Immediately above the Air Force procurement classified line sits 'SPECIAL UPDATE PROGRAM' at $1.178 billion in FY2026 - a titled line that discloses nothing. For comparison, the published FY2026 request was $81.9 billion for the National Intelligence Program and $33.6 billion for the Military Intelligence Program, a combined $115.5 billion. No public document maps the $95.9 billion of classified defense line items onto the $115.5 billion of intelligence programme aggregate, and no public document accounts for the difference. That reconciliation, if it exists, is in the classified annex.

gaps: The contents of the classified annex to the annual Defense Appropriations Act and of the classified Schedule of Authorizations to the Intelligence Authorization Act. These are the two documents that would answer the entire question, and both are given the force of law by public statute (Sec. 8006(a) of P.L. 119-75; Sec. 6102(a) of P.L. 119-60) while being unpublishable by statutory command.

Whether any Inspector General has ever conducted a compliance review of section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA - the prohibition on UAP-related independent research and development being an allowable indirect cost. The provision is permanent law codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373 note; no published DoD OIG, IC IG or DCAA product examines compliance with it. This is the single most answerable open question on this board: a committee could simply ask.

The identity of the contractors, if any, that have charged UAP-related work to Independent Research and Development accounts. DCAA audits IR&D cost allowability and its working papers are agency records; the DoD Instruction 3204.01 technical interchange meeting record is also an agency record.

Whether any activity relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena has been the subject of a 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver removing it from the annual SAP report to the defense committees, and whether any such activity has ever been the subject of a Sec. 8009 thirty-day pre-initiation notice.

The recipient of the $26.92 billion Other Procurement, Air Force 'CLASSIFIED PROGRAMS' line (FY2026 line 077A) and the content of the adjacent $1.178 billion 'SPECIAL UPDATE PROGRAM' line. The pass-through attribution to national reconnaissance activity is inference from account history and magnitude, not documentation.

The reconciliation between the roughly $95.9 billion of classified line items in the FY2026 defense funding tables and the $115.5 billion combined NIP and MIP request for the same year. No public document maps one onto the other or explains the gap.

The names of the Department of Defense officials who approached FASAB in August 2016 to request what became SFFAS 56, and the seventeen comment letters received on the exposure draft between 14 December 2017 and 16 March 2018. FASAB's deliberative record - exposure draft, comment letters, board meeting minutes and transcripts - is public and has never been systematically read against this question.

Whether FASAB has issued any Interpretation of SFFAS 56 under paragraph 8(c), which authorises modifications beyond those listed in paragraph 9. Paragraph 13 forbids the government-wide report to identify which Interpretations were applied, so the existence and content of any such Interpretation cannot be inferred from the financial statements.

Which entities have actually applied SFFAS 56 and to what amounts. Paragraph 12 expressly forbids disclosure of application, so this is unknowable from the financial statements by design; only a cleared auditor or a congressional committee with access to the unmodified reports could establish it.

The underlying journal voucher detail behind DODIG-2016-113's $2.8 trillion and $6.5 trillion figures and behind the FY2025 audit's $859 billion. The OIG reports are summaries; the transaction-level records exist in DFAS systems and have never been sought by FOIA or subpoena in connection with this question.

Which independent public accounting firm will assume the group auditor role for the Department's financial statements in FY2027, under what contract vehicle, and what becomes of the working-paper custody chain when the group auditor is a contractor rather than the Office of Inspector General.
The classified portion of David Grusch's testimony and of the ICIG's July 2022 credible-and-urgent determination, which is where the financial specifics he declined to give in open session reside.

Whether the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform has ever, in writing, connected its July 2023 UAP hearing to its May 2026 Department of War financial management hearing. Both are its own proceedings; no published question, letter or report joins them.

The dates of Platte B. Moring III's assumption of office as Inspector General and of Michael Powers's acting service as Under Secretary (Comptroller), and whether either is Senate-confirmed. The Department's own biography pages do not state it.

Any record of expenditure under 50 U.S.C. 3510(b) - the CIA's unvouchered account - relating to material recovery or exploitation. By statute the Director's certificate is the entire accounting record and 'shall be deemed a sufficient voucher'; if the programme was ever financed this way, no further record was ever required to exist.
